entries.label: US-China relations
entries.summary: US unemployment and Chinese growth push the two powers toward friction.
entries.quote: The biggest risk for 2010 comes from the point at which these three trends converge: US-China relations.
entries.note: Quote is from the introduction, not the section body.

entries.label: Iran
entries.summary: Iran under pressure at home and abroad has more reason to provoke conflict.
entries.quote: By far the biggest purely geopolitical risk in 2010 comes from Iran.

entries.label: European fiscal divergence
entries.summary: Uneven fiscal politics bring political risk back to the eurozone.
entries.quote: Political risk returns to the Eurozone in an important way this year, with the consequent blurring of the distinction between “mature” and “emerging” markets.

entries.label: US financial regulation
entries.summary: Election-year politics shape US and European financial reform.
entries.quote: On balance, 2010 is looking like a tougher year for President Obama than 2009 proved to be.
entries.note: The printed opening sentence sets the political context, not the regulation risk itself.

entries.label: Japan
entries.summary: Japan's new ruling party governs weakly and risks another lost decade.
entries.quote: What happens when the ruling party loses power in a one-party state? You get a zero-party state.

entries.label: Climate change
entries.summary: After Copenhagen a global climate treaty is years away and conflict grows.
entries.quote: Before Copenhagen, the prevailing presumption was that 2010 would be the year when a global treaty, including the United States, China and India, really got done.

entries.label: Brazil
entries.summary: Brazil's economic boom lowers the quality of policymaking.
entries.quote: After years of being wildly bullish on Brazil, we’re in for a bump.

entries.label: India-Pakistan
entries.summary: India-Pakistan tension, not Afghanistan, is the main South Asia risk.
entries.quote: South Asia is still a morass in 2010.
entries.note: Section heading prints 'India-Pakistan (no, not Afghanistan)'; the risk list prints 'India-Pakistan'.

entries.label: Eastern Europe, elections & unemployment
entries.summary: High unemployment and elections raise political risk in Eastern Europe.
entries.quote: Coming out of global recession, historically high levels of unemployment are a critical factor in a solid majority of the world’s economies.

entries.label: Turkey
entries.summary: Domestic fights and foreign policy put Turkey at risk.
entries.quote: There’s very little "country risk" in the top 10 this year, but trends in Turkey are sufficiently worrisome that it deserves a slot.

entries.label: Iraq
entries.summary: Eurasia Group expects investment and oil, not security, to be Iraq's story.
entries.quote: But the real story is going to be a moderate government, growing geopolitical influence, and the most exciting new investment opportunities the region has seen in a decade.
entries.note: Red herrings are not ranked; rank is the printed order.

entries.label: The Persian Gulf
entries.summary: Eurasia Group expects the Gulf to stay stable despite Dubai's problems.
entries.quote: Iraq’s gain trumps Dubai’s loss in the Persian Gulf, and the rest of the region is doing just fine.
entries.note: Red herrings are not ranked; rank is the printed order.

entries.label: Russia
entries.summary: Eurasia Group expects Russia to get through the downturn and look stable.
entries.quote: This year, Russia gets through the downturn and starts to look stable again.
entries.note: Red herrings are not ranked; rank is the printed order.

entries.label: The dollar
entries.summary: Eurasia Group expects the dollar to keep its reserve-currency role.
entries.quote: The status of the dollar as the world’s reserve currency is much stronger than the hyped commentary.
entries.note: Red herrings are not ranked; rank is the printed order.

entries.label: New York and London
entries.summary: Eurasia Group does not expect finance to leave New York and London.
entries.quote: All this fear about "finance" running away from New York and London--because of regulatory burdens or growth outside the developed world--is misplaced.
entries.note: Red herrings are not ranked; rank is the printed order.
